title: fix(feeds): emit PlusPlus chapters when audio_chapters is empty
body:
**Detail bug report:** [View on Detail](https://app.detail.dev/org_725d4daf-5c28-4be1-b98e-9ff91ae58deb/bugs/bug_eb182825-4955-4743-951b-6bb60473b3c4)

## Bug

The PlusPlus RSS feed (`Xml.Plusplus`) and PlusPlus-enabled personalized feeds (`Xml.Feed` with `plusplus: true`) silently dropped **all** chapter data whenever an episode's `audio_chapters` list was empty — even when `plusplus_chapters` was populated and a `plusplus_file` was present. Premium subscribers lost chapter navigation (seeking, skip-to-topic, deep-linking) for affected feed items; the feed rendered without error and the `<item>` stayed valid RSS, so the only symptom was an empty/absent chapters panel in clients.

Root cause: the `chapters/1` guard `defp chapters(%{audio_chapters: []}), do: nil` was copied from `Xml.Podcast` (the public audio-only feed, where gating on `audio_chapters` is correct) during the 2024 builder migration and applied unchanged to the PlusPlus feed — whose body clause routes to `plusplus_chapters`. The guard returned `nil` before the routing `if` could run, so both `<podcast:chapters>` and the inline `<psc:chapters>` were dropped from the `<item>`. The same guard existed in `Xml.Feed`.

## Fix

Only suppress chapters when there are genuinely none to emit; the routing bodies (which already correctly prefer `plusplus_chapters` when a `plusplus_file` exists) are unchanged.

- `plusplus.ex` — two guards → `nil`: `%{audio_chapters: [], plusplus_chapters: []}` and `%{audio_chapters: [], plusplus_file: nil}` (audio-only items with no PlusPlus cut).
- `feed.ex` — two guards split on `feed.plusplus`: `%{plusplus: true}, %{audio_chapters: [], plusplus_chapters: []}` and `%{plusplus: false}, %{audio_chapters: []}`.

The guards are split rather than collapsed to the single `%{audio_chapters: [], plusplus_chapters: []}` field because the PlusPlus feed aggregates all published episodes (including audio-only ones with no `plusplus_file`), and a single-field guard would leak an empty `<podcast:chapters>` link + empty `<psc:chapters>` for those items and for non-PlusPlus feed items. The two-clause form preserves the prior suppression for those edges.

## Testing

- Added `test/changelog_web/xml/plusplus_chapters_test.exs` covering the regression for both `Xml.Plusplus` and `Xml.Feed` (PlusPlus chapters emitted when `audio_chapters` is empty but `plusplus_chapters` is present), the both-empty suppression, the audio-only-with-stray-`plusplus_chapters` edge, and the non-PlusPlus feed suppression.
- Confirmed the suite is load-bearing: reverting the guards makes exactly the two regression tests fail; restoring the fix returns all to green.
- Routine checks pass: `mix compile --warnings-as-errors`, `mix format --check-formatted`, the existing feed controller suite, and the full test suite (no regressions).
- End-to-end (unversioned, throwaway test): exercised the real HTTP routes (`/plusplus/<slug>/feed`, `/<podcast>/feed`, `/<podcast>/<episode>/chapters?pp=true`) against DB-persisted episodes in the bug state. The PlusPlus `<item>` rendered both `<podcast:chapters …?pp=true>` and `<psc:chapters><psc:chapter title="Intro++"/></psc:chapters>`; the public podcast feed's `<item>` for the same episode correctly omitted chapters (no PlusPlus title leak); the `?pp=true` chapters JSON returned the PlusPlus chapter.
- Feed validation: `xmllint` confirmed well-formed XML; a structural validator (lxml, checking RSS 2.0 + Podcast Namespace 1.0 + Podlove Simple Chapters conformance) passed; the W3C Feed Validator reported no chapter-related errors (only expected test-environment artifacts — `localhost` image URLs from the test endpoint). Two other named external validators could not be run: castfeedvalidator.com exposes only a JavaScript form with no URL/CLI API, and polator.net failed DNS resolution (NXDOMAIN).

---

title: Enforce unique episode-backed news item identities
body:
## Production Rollout Approved
Operator approved the exact candidate and normal CI migration/deploy sequence on September 8 after successful CI, CodeRabbit review and fresh read-only production preflight. Publishing is held through post-deploy verification.

## What And Why
Add a database guarantee for the canonical episode-backed news item identity.
Application publish paths already serialize on the episode and reconcile the
existing row; this index protects against future writers bypassing that path.

- Unique index on `news_items.object_id` where the value matches
  `^[1-9][0-9]*:[1-9][0-9]*$`, covering every podcast, type, status and feed mode.
- Keep nulls and historical non-episode namespaces outside the guarantee, and
  retain the existing general lookup index.
- Use a transactional migration with 2s lock timeout and 20s statement timeout.
  It briefly blocks writes during the build. No concurrent-index recovery state,
  automatic cleanup or silent adoption of a same-name index.
- Preserve the legacy duplicate-read test by dropping the index only within that
  non-async sandbox transaction; rollback restores it.

No notification/queue redesign, dependency update or application locking change.
Blind conflicting writes are rejected; the supported publish path stays idempotent.
The local migration timeouts do not bound Ecto's earlier migration-lock setup.

## Validation
- 74 focused tests passed, including real multi-connection publish races.
- 989 full-suite tests passed on local PostgreSQL 17.9.
- Touched-file format and whitespace checks passed.
- Actual Ecto migration rehearsed on an isolated PostgreSQL 16.15 branch:
  up/down/up, repeat migration, duplicate insert/update rejection, historical
  namespace compatibility, duplicate-build failure rollback, lock timeout/retry
  and same-name index collision rejection.
- Final rehearsal index was unique/ready/valid with no duplicate groups.
- Direct code review found no blocking issue in this candidate. CI passed all 989 tests; CodeRabbit completed with no actionable findings.

## Delivery Contract
Governing local artifacts: PEP-0011 / SPEC-0001 (private operational evidence
remains local, not included in this PR).

Head: `59cf9e524dd7c8b3432453bdca2a971b35e1e994`.
Base at review: `acc6a3249f24e55c37876deef3438474987346f5` (`master`).
Intended merge strategy: squash, only after separate approval of the exact
candidate and production migration window. Retain branches until cleanup is
separately approved. Any candidate change invalidates the current review.

## Summary

This PR makes episode publishing idempotent so duplicate publish attempts converge on one canonical episode-backed news item instead of creating duplicate `news_items` rows, duplicate queue entries, or duplicate first-publish side effects.

The production symptom was an `Ecto.MultipleResultsError` on episode pages when `Episode.load_news_item/1` expected at most one `news_items` row for an episode-backed `object_id` but found two. The likely trigger was duplicate publish flow execution, such as concurrent/double-submit admin publish requests or overlapping publish writers.

## What changed

- Locks the episode row during publish/reconcile with `FOR UPDATE` so concurrent publish attempts serialize on the episode.
- Reconciles the canonical episode-backed news item instead of blindly inserting a new one.
- Uses earliest `inserted_at`, then `id`, as the canonical item policy.
- Keeps non-feed-only visibility from being demoted by a later feed-only retry.
- Dedupes queue append behavior with `NewsQueue.append_once/1`.
- Queues first-transition notes push only once.
- Moves external side effects that do not need to be inside the transaction, including search refresh and guest thanks handling, until after the publish transaction commits.
- Updates `Episode.get_news_item/1` to select the canonical item instead of crashing when duplicate episode-backed rows already exist.

## Verification

Local non-Docker verification passed:

- `git diff --check`
- `mix format --check-formatted ...` for touched files
- `mix compile`
- Focused tests: `79 tests, 0 failures`
- Full suite: `968 tests, 0 failures`
- `af validate pep-0009`
- `af validate spec-0001`

Known local caveat: `mise run ci` cannot currently complete on this Apple Silicon machine through Docker. Native arm64 Docker fails because the runtime Dockerfile downloads `linux-x64` Node/fnox artifacts. Forcing `DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=linux/amd64` gets farther but segfaults during `mix deps.compile` for `otel_http` under emulation. Remote Namespace CI is the intended source of truth for this repo's Docker CI path.

## Database follow-up

This PR intentionally does not add the database unique invariant yet.

Recommended post-deploy sequence:

1. Merge and deploy this app-side idempotency fix first.
2. Observe production for duplicate Zulip notifications, Sentry `Ecto.MultipleResultsError`, and new duplicate episode-backed `news_items` rows.
3. Run a read-only production audit for duplicate episode-backed `object_id` groups.
4. Clean existing duplicates, keeping the canonical earliest row.
5. Add the database constraint/index in a separate small PR/deploy.

The app fix should land before the DB constraint so old duplicate writes do not turn into publish failures under the existing production code path.

title: Replace `asdf`, `just`, `dagger` & `direnv` with `mise` + `fnox`
body:
The local dev + CI/CD stack had grown into four tools: `asdf` (versions), `just` (tasks), `direnv` (env), and `dagger` via a `1,194`-line Go SDK (CI/CD), each needing its own orientation before you could contribute. The `dagger` Go SDK was pinned to a ~3-year-old release (v0.6.4, July 2023) that needed Go 1.20 + a running engine just to run CI locally. Use it or lose it. We chose lose it.

This PR replaces all of it with `mise` + `fnox` (both by @jdx):
- `mise` handles tool versions, tasks, and environment
- `fnox` handles secrets via 1Password

Two tools, clean separation of concerns, and the same command locally and in CI: `mise run ci`

## At a glance

```
Before                            After
──────                            ─────
.tool-versions (asdf)        ──→  mise.toml [tools]
.envrc (direnv)              ──→  mise.toml [env]
justfile (25 recipes)        ──→  mise-tasks/ (file tasks)
magefiles/ (1,194 lines Go)  ──→  docker/ (3 Dockerfiles)
envrc.secrets.op / env.op    ──→  fnox.toml (1Password references)
7 GitHub Actions secrets     ──→  1 secret (OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN)
```

Most of the Go was a programmatic Dockerfile generator: every `WithExec(["apt-get", "install"])` was a `RUN` waiting to break free. The `.tool-versions` parser, env-var wrappers, and custom exit codes only existed because Go needed them. `mise` + `bash` give them for free.

## The CI pipeline

`mise run ci` runs identically on a local machine and in GitHub Actions:

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  1. build runtime image                    │
│           │                                │
│     ┌─────┴─────┐                          │
│     ▼           ▼                          │
│  2. test     3. build prod     (parallel)  │
│     │           │                          │
│     └─────┬─────┘                          │
│           ▼                                │
│  4. publish runtime + prod    (if master)  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Parallelism via mise's built-in `:::` operator means no extra runtime. `docker buildx` is the engine everywhere: local daemon, GitHub-hosted, or Namespace.so remote builders. Because a remote builder can't `FROM` a locally-built image, `build-runtime` pushes the runtime to the zero-auth `nscr.io` registry on Namespace (and `--load`s it into the local daemon on GitHub); `test` and `build-prod` then `FROM` that runtime.

## By the numbers

```
81 files changed       Go code:      1,194 → 0
+2,816 / -2,353        Tools:            4 → 2
Net: -463 lines        GH secrets:       7 → 1
                       CI command:      43 → 2 characters
```

956 tests pass both natively (`mise run test`) and in Docker (`mise run docker:test`).

## Beyond the 1:1 port

The first commit was a straight migration. Everything below was built on top after exercising every task end-to-end and fixing what the port left broken or incomplete.

**Tasks organised into three tiers**, grouped by domain not by tool. Everyday tasks need no credentials (`db:*`, `deps:*`); a dedicated `team:*` tier gathers everything privileged (1Password, Neon, GHCR, Fly); `vm:*` covers VM lifecycle. A shared `_lib.sh` makes every team task fail with a "run `mise team:secrets:load`" hint instead of a bare `must be set`. Docker image metadata (OCI labels + manifest annotations, via `buildx imagetools create`) now matches what Dagger published to GHCR, and buildx cache mounts restore the per-layer caching Dagger's volumes used to provide. The `deps:bump` and `deps:install` tasks were rewritten to query actual upstream availability (only versions with prebuilt binaries for `ubuntu-24.04`) so you can't pick a version that fails to install.

**Secrets out of GitHub, and a clean split between secret and non-secret config.** GitHub Actions needs just one repository secret, `OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN`, used only by the upstream-`master` publish & deploy steps (`HONEYCOMB_GITHUB_ACTIONS_WORKFLOWS` lives on the separate trace workflow). Every former secret (`GHCR_PASSWORD`, `FLY_API_TOKEN`, `R2_*`, `ZULIP_BOT_API_KEY`) is read from 1Password by fnox at publish/deploy or app runtime. Low-entropy values that aren't secrets (`AWS_REGION`, the prod db name) moved out of fnox into `mise.toml`/code defaults — loading them via fnox was redacting those strings from unrelated output.

**Fork-friendly CI + a new app instance.** Build & test run fully **unauthenticated**, so any fork or PR gets a green build with no secrets — production config reads every value at runtime with defaults, and tests run against a local Postgres, so neither needs credentials. Publish & deploy are opt-in via a `DEPLOY_FROM_REPO` repo variable (compared against the live `github.com/owner/repo`); nothing hardcodes `thechangelog/changelog.com` anymore. `ship_it.yml` runs exactly one runner via complementary `if:` conditions: Namespace.so when available, else GitHub-hosted. Adds the `changelog-2026-06-14` Fly instance (Machines API, `[http_service]` + `[processes]`, `APP_INSTANCE=experimental` so Oban queues stay empty) and a `new-fly-app-instance` skill — a human-in-the-loop runbook to create an instance, validate the whole pipeline **from a fork first** (both runners, confirming blue-green deploys), and promote it to production — replacing the prose walkthrough in `INFRASTRUCTURE.md`.

**A security & robustness pass over the migrated stack.** CI runs least-privilege: the `GITHUB_TOKEN` is granted only `contents: read`, `secrets: inherit` is replaced by passing just the one token the workflows use, and `persist-credentials: false` keeps it out of `.git/config` before untrusted (incl. fork-PR) build code runs. The prod container runs as a non-root `app` user with a writable `HOME`. The runtime image verifies every third-party download instead of trusting the transport — node against `SHASUMS256.txt`, fnox against the sha256 in `mise.lock`, yarn against a pinned sha256 cross-checked with Yarn's GPG signature. Runtime scripts were hardened too: `app.start` exec's the server so it's PID 1 and receives Fly's `SIGTERM` for graceful shutdown; `on.deploy` runs under `set -euo pipefail` so a failed asset upload aborts before `ecto.migrate`.

**`[env]` defaults via POSIX `${VAR:-default}`.** Following @jdx's review (thank you!), the `[env]` defaults now use `env_shell_expand = true` with POSIX `${VAR:-default}` instead of the longer Tera `get_env`/coalesce blocks. Earlier mise releases didn't coalesce empty strings (only unset) under shell expansion, which our CI relies on since it forwards repo vars unconditionally (an unset variable arrives as `""`). jdx fixed both empty-coalescing and recursive fallback expansion in [jdx/mise#10445](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/10445) (shipped `2026.6.10`); background in [discussion #10444](https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/10444). Behaviour is identical: a fork overrides `IMAGE_OWNER` / `APP_PROD_INSTANCE` by setting the repo variable; empty and unset both fall back to the default.

**VM workflow helpers + `VIBE.md`.** The `vm:*` tasks (`incus`, `image`, `launch`, `blueprint`, `destroy`, `keep`) are the old `justfile` recipes that the migration had dropped, now converted and fixed. New fish functions collapse SSH → working Claude session into a single command, and `VIBE.md` was rewritten to use `mise vm:*` throughout (LazyVim instead of unmaintained NvChad, `claude` installed via mise).

**Housekeeping.** Remove the long-dead `fly.io/changelog-2024-01-12` manifest; pin all third-party GitHub Actions to commit SHAs (a mutable `@v4` tag can change under a fixed ref; a SHA can't), with a source link above each `uses:` so the SHA is verifiable.

---

Validated end-to-end from a fork (`gerhard/changelog.com`) on both runners — Namespace and GitHub-hosted — before opening this PR: build → test → publish → deploy to `changelog-2026-06-14`, running healthy across two regions.

title: Make our ship_it.yml GHA workflow resilient
body: ## TL;DR --- As you already know, we use Dagger for CI/CD. By default, this runs on Fly.io (via Docker). In some cases, this can fail. The last failure was when DNS resolution stopped working after the Docker instance was auto-upgraded from apps v1 -> v2 (a.k.a. Fly.io machines): https://github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/actions/runs/5673476702/attempts/1 As a temporary fix, we had to delete some secrets and re-run the job. The job ran on GHA free runners & failed for genuine reasons 6 mins later: https://github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/actions/runs/5673476702/job/15395264391 While running on the free GHA runners can be 3x-8x slower, it's a good fall-back. You heard us mention on multiple occasions: "always have redundancies in place". Since we already have multiple CI runtimes in place (Fly.io, K8s), let's make our GHA workflow resilient by: - Run on our preferred back-end by default (Dagger on Fly.io) - ✅ If it succeeds, we are done - ❌ If it fails, fallback to running on the free GitHub runners - In forks, use free GitHub runners by default (we cannot share `secrets`) While this means that a workflow which fails for genuine reasons will fail twice for us (1. Dagger on Fly.io, 2. Dagger on GitHub), it seems like a better place to improve from. This change goes one step further. We are using a third back-end: Dagger on K8s. This uses a self-hosted GitHub runner on K8s which is already integrated with Dagger. For now, we are using it just to see how the CI part compares to our primary setup (Dagger on Fly.io). We are not using Dagger on K8s to deploy the app. Let's see how this setup behaves over a few weeks/months before we consider taking it further. Part of this, we also improved on how we check for Fly.io connectivity. --- Things that could be improved in follow-ups: - the workflow should succeed if the `dagger-on-github-fallback` job succeeds - currently it fails if `dagger-on-fly-docker` fails - add `dagger-on-k8s` job as secondary fallback - GitHub Actions is currently missing https://github.com/actions/runner/issues/1665 - maybe leverage a Dagger cache that works in forks too 😉 - https://github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/pull/471

In order to minimize bugs and differences in behaviour between dev & prod, we want to be running the same runtime dependency versions (e.g. Erlang, Elixir, Node.js & PostgreSQL) in both environments.

In development, we are using https://asdf-vm.com/ to manage runtime dependencies. This means that with a single command - `asdf install` - everyone working with our codebase can have the same dependencies installed. Currently these are:
- direnv 2.32.2
- elixir 1.14.4
- erlang 25.3.2
- golang 1.20.4
- nodejs 18.16.0
- yarn 1.22.19
- postgres 14.1
- flyctl 0.1.8

We used to manually edit these versions in our CI/CD pipeline. Since we are using Dagger for CI/CD, this was no big deal since our pipeline is just code. But since it is code, we could go one step further. Our pipeline could read the `.tool-versions` file and use that information to build the container image that gets deployed to production. That's exactly what this change does.

The only runtime dependency version that does not exist in `.tool-versions` is the OS - Ubuntu 22.04 in production. This is a reasonable limitation that we could improve as a follow-up. title: Increase connections limit for our Fly.io app instance
body: ~18:50 UTC time Pingdom started reporting `Socket timeout, unable to connect to server` for our Fly.io app instance: On closer inspection, the app instance [hit the default `25` connections limit](https://fly.io/docs/reference/configuration/#services-concurrency): [![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/3342/197419463-7f0a0ee5-2bf0-4a4a-a6d2-97f6e851fe7d.png)](https://fly-metrics.net/d/fly-app/fly-app?orgId=23559&from=1666546656028&to=1666558998886&viewPanel=1) As a result, the app instance stopped accepting any new connections, and therefore serving any traffic: This is peculiar, since everything looked normal from the CDN (Fastly) perspective: Anyhow, `25` concurrent connections is a super low limit and it was obvious that we needed to bump it up. That's what this PR does. FTR, the change has been already applied via `fly deploy`. Notice the app concurrency: - after this change was rolled out @ 19:50 - number of connections growing linearly to > 450 over the span of 1h - the app concurrency resetting itself to a normal level afterwards While there was a secondary smaller spike (maxed out at 15 connections), it was nothing like what happened previously. Neither https://status.fastly.com/, nor https://status.flyio.net/ show any incident during this period. I am wondering what metrics/logs are we missing to figure out whether: 1. This was a Fastly issue, maybe keeping connections open for longer than they needed to 2. This was a Fly issue, where connections were not being terminate properly 3. A mix of both 🤷‍♂️ ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Fastly CDN] --> |TCP| B{Fly Proxy} B --> |TCP| C(Phoenix app instance) ``` WDYT @mrkurt? If this looks good to you @jerodsanto, ship it!

title: Deploy & use Docker Engine running on Fly.io
body:
Before this, GitHub Actions was using a Docker Engine running on a bare metal host. We were connecting to it via Tailscale. This was OK as a stop-gap, but we ran into issues with:
- `TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY` max 90d TTL - [Generate auth key](https://login.tailscale.com/admin/settings/keys) +Reusable +Ephemeral
- `dagger-buildkitd` default container getting upgraded by a newer dagger CLI (I was using the same Docker Engine)
- `changelog_test_postgres` container failing to TCP port (another PostgreSQL was already running)

This introduces a dedicated Docker Engine running on Fly.io. It has a cache that persists between runs & is faster than the default GitHub Actions free runner (4 CPUs vs 2 CPUs). The PR includes:

- Upgrade fly cli to latest in 2022.fly
- Deploy Docker Engine on Fly.io
- Use Fly.io Docker Engine in prod_image workflow
- Only deploy the master branch

I am looking forward to use [Fly machines](https://fly.io/blog/fly-machines/) and spin up this Docker Engine... on the fly 🛫

title: ✈️ Migrate changelog.com to Fly.io ✈️
body:
This is the story of migrating changelog.com from LKE to fly.io, [a PaaS where _Phoenix screams_](https://fly.io/blog/how-we-got-to-liveview/). The main reason was to challenge assumptions (mostly mine) and experiment with doing things differently, in a simpler way. I am genuinely curious to discover what we will actually miss most from our Kubernetes setup, what alternatives are there (some may be better!), and most importantly how well does this actually work in practice. I still think that `AND` propositions are better than `OR`, and while I don't rule Kubernetes from our future, now is a good time to spring clean and shake things up a bit 😉 Also, I am heeding wise advice, and migrating Postgres to [a managed fly.io one](https://fly.io/docs/reference/postgres/): Most of the changes I ran imperatively, by issuing `fly` commands. While I tried to capture some of them in the latest implementation of [Dagger 0.2.0](https://dagger.io), at some point I started getting slowed down because I was trying to reconcile two things at once. I have since shifted focus to `fly` only in order to achieve the primary goal of migrating changelog.com to fly.io quicker. The backstory is that we are currently running on Linode Kubernetes Engine 1.20 which will be forcefully migrated to 1.21 on March 17, 2022 (so in less than 48 hours). K8s 1.20 is EOL and upgrades + security patches are no longer available. While we started a 1.22 K8s LKE cluster in the [2022 dir](https://github.com/thechangelog/changelog.com/tree/e67acd1d054ef2277b2a1a82317a607884ac2202/2022), we didn't finish that migration - life happened - and at this point the quickest thing is to migrate to fly.io. In all honesty, we have been talking about this for months: Ship It [#44](https://changelog.com/shipit/44), [#43](https://changelog.com/shipit/43), [#40](https://changelog.com/shipit/40) & [#31](https://changelog.com/shipit/31). This is the simplest thing right now. We will make some new friends - 👋🏻 @mrkurt @chrismccord @brainlid 👋🏻 - and most likely have a great story to share.
